lessons.title: Key Performance Indicators for Farms
lessons.body: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) are simple numbers that tell you how well your farm is doing. You don't need a computer or an accountant to track them. Start with five basic KPIs: yield per hectare, cost per hectare, gross margin per hectare, labour productivity, and water use efficiency. For example, if you grow maize on 2 hectares and harvest 6 tonnes, your yield is 3 tonnes per hectare. If your total cost was 1,200,000 shillings, your cost per hectare is 600,000 shillings. Gross margin is total income minus variable costs (seeds, fertiliser, casual labour). If you sold maize for 1,800,000 shillings and variable costs were 700,000 shillings, your gross margin is 1,100,000 shillings, or 550,000 per hectare. Labour productivity: if you and two workers spent 200 hours total and produced 6 tonnes, that's 30 kg per labour hour. Water use efficiency: if you used 500,000 litres of irrigation water, you produced 12 kg of maize per 1,000 litres. Write these numbers in a simple notebook each season. Compare them over time. If your yield per hectare drops from 3 to 2.5 tonnes, investigate whyâmaybe poor seed, pests, or low rainfall. If your cost per hectare rises but yield stays same, find cheaper inputs or reduce waste. Share these KPIs with your family or workers so everyone knows the targets. In Africa, many farmers use mobile apps like FarmDrive or Ushahidi to record KPIs, but a paper record works just as well. The goal is to make decisions based on facts, not guesses.

lessons.title: Enterprise Budgeting and Analysis
lessons.body: An enterprise budget is a plan for one crop or livestock activity. It lists all income and costs for that enterprise, so you can see if it makes a profit. For example, a one-hectare tomato enterprise in Kenya. Expected income: if you harvest 15,000 kg and sell at 60 KES per kg, total income is 900,000 KES. Variable costs: seeds (20,000), fertiliser (80,000), pesticides (40,000), casual labour (150,000), transport to market (30,000), packaging (20,000). Total variable costs = 340,000 KES. Gross margin = 900,000 - 340,000 = 560,000 KES. Fixed costs: land rent (50,000), depreciation on tools (10,000), interest on loan (20,000). Total fixed costs = 80,000 KES. Net profit = 560,000 - 80,000 = 480,000 KES. Now compare with a maize enterprise: income 200,000 KES, variable costs 80,000 KES, gross margin 120,000 KES, fixed costs 40,000 KES, net profit 80,000 KES. Clearly tomatoes are more profitable per hectare, but they need more labour and water. Enterprise budgets help you decide what to plant. Use a simple table in a notebook or a free spreadsheet on your phone. Include columns for quantity, unit price, and total. Update your budget each season with real prices from your local market. If you have several enterprises (e.g., maize, beans, chickens), make a budget for each and compare gross margins per hectare or per animal. This shows where to invest your limited land and money. In Africa, organisations like AGRA and local extension officers can provide template budgets. Always include a 10% contingency for unexpected costs like drought or disease.

lessons.title: Partial Budgeting for Decisions
lessons.body: Partial budgeting is a tool to compare two options when you only change part of your farm. For example, should you switch from local maize seed to hybrid seed? You only change the seed, not the whole farm. List the changes: added costs (hybrid seed costs 15,000 KES per hectare vs local seed 5,000 KES, so extra cost 10,000 KES). Added income (hybrid yields 4 tonnes per hectare vs local 2 tonnes, so extra 2 tonnes. At 30,000 KES per tonne, extra income = 60,000 KES). Reduced costs (none in this case). Reduced income (none). Net change = (added income + reduced costs) - (added costs + reduced income) = (60,000 + 0) - (10,000 + 0) = +50,000 KES. So hybrid seed is better by 50,000 KES per hectare. Another example: should you buy a sprayer for 40,000 KES instead of hiring labour to spray? Hiring costs 10,000 KES per season. Sprayer lasts 5 years, so annual depreciation 8,000 KES. Added cost: depreciation 8,000 KES. Reduced cost: labour 10,000 KES. Net change = 10,000 - 8,000 = +2,000 KES per year. But you also need to consider repairs and fuel. If repairs cost 3,000 KES per year, net change = 10,000 - (8,000+3,000) = -1,000 KES, so hiring is better. Partial budgeting forces you to list only what changes. Use a simple four-column table: Added Income, Reduced Costs, Added Costs, Reduced Income. Sum each side and compare. If the left side (income + reduced costs) is bigger than the right side (costs + reduced income), the change is profitable. This method is quick and works for decisions like adding a new crop, changing fertiliser, or renting extra land. Always use realistic local prices and yields.

lessons.title: Cash Flow Projections
lessons.body: A cash flow projection shows when money comes in and goes out each month. It helps you avoid running out of cash, even if your farm is profitable on paper. Start with a simple table: months across the top, categories down the side. Categories: cash sales (e.g., milk, eggs, vegetables), other income (loans, grants), cash expenses (seeds, feed, labour, fuel, loan repayments), and net cash flow (income minus expenses). For example, a small poultry farm in Ghana. In January, you spend 2,000 GHS on chicks and feed, but no sales yet. Net cash flow = -2,000 GHS. In February, spend 1,500 GHS on feed, sell 500 GHS of eggs. Net = -1,000 GHS. In March, spend 1,500 GHS, sell 2,000 GHS eggs and 3,000 GHS mature birds. Net = +3,500 GHS. By March, you have recovered. But if you had a loan repayment of 2,000 GHS in February, your net would be -3,000 GHS, and you might need a short-term loan or savings. To project, use last year's records or ask other farmers. Be conservative: underestimate income, overestimate costs. Include all cash outflows: not just variable costs but also family living expenses, school fees, and loan interest. Update your projection every month with actual figures. If you see a negative month coming, plan ahead: delay a purchase, sell some assets, or arrange credit. Tools: a notebook with 12 columns, or a free app like Excel or Google Sheets on your phone. In Africa, many farmers use M-Pesa or Airtel Money statements to track cash. Remember, cash flow is not profit. You can have a profitable season but still run out of cash if you spend too much before harvest. Always keep a cash reserve of at least 10% of annual expenses.

lessons.title: Benchmarking Against Industry Standards
lessons.body: Benchmarking means comparing your farm's performance to others in your area or to industry averages. It shows where you are doing well and where you can improve. Start by finding standard figures. For example, in Kenya, the average maize yield for smallholders is about 2 tonnes per hectare. If you get 3 tonnes, you are above average. If you get 1.5 tonnes, you are below. Where to find benchmarks? Local extension officers, farmer cooperatives, research stations (e.g., KALRO in Kenya, IITA in Nigeria), and agricultural ministries publish average yields, costs, and prices. Also, talk to successful neighbours. For livestock, benchmarks might be milk per cow per day (e.g., 10 litres for local breeds, 20 litres for improved). For poultry, eggs per hen per year (e.g., 200 for layers). For costs, benchmark your cost per hectare or per animal. If your cost per hectare for maize is 60,000 KES and the average is 50,000 KES, you are spending too muchâmaybe on fertiliser or labour. Compare your gross margin per hectare. If yours is 30,000 KES and average is 40,000 KES, you need to increase yield or reduce costs. Use a simple table: your figure, benchmark figure, difference. Then ask why. Maybe your soil is poor, or you plant late. Set a target to close the gap. For example, if your milk yield is 8 litres per cow and benchmark is 12, aim for 10 next year by improving feed and veterinary care. Benchmarking is not about copying others blindlyâyour conditions may differ. But it gives a reality check. In Africa, the African Farmers' Association and AGRA publish benchmark reports. Also, mobile platforms like iCow in Kenya provide benchmarks via SMS. Always use local benchmarks, not from Europe or America, because costs and yields differ greatly.

lessons.title: Creating Reports for Lenders and Investors
lessons.body: Lenders (banks, microfinance) and investors (partners, grants) need clear reports to decide whether to give you money. Your report should include: a one-page summary, your farm records, and your analysis. Start with a cover page: your name, farm name, date, and purpose (e.g., loan application for 500,000 KES). Then a summary: what you do, your location, how long you've been farming, and how much you need. Next, include your production records: hectares, yields, livestock numbers. Show your financial records: income statement (profit and loss) for the last 2-3 years, and a cash flow projection for the next 12 months. Use simple tables. For example, income statement: Year 1 income 1,200,000 KES, expenses 800,000 KES, profit 400,000 KES. Year 2 income 1,500,000 KES, expenses 900,000 KES, profit 600,000 KES. Then include your enterprise budgets and partial budgets to show you understand your costs. Lenders want to see that you can repay. Show your debt repayment plan: how much you will pay each month, from which income. Investors want to see growth potential and return on investment. Include your KPIs and benchmarking: e.g., your yield is 3 tonnes per hectare vs average 2, so you are efficient. Add photos of your farm, receipts, and bank statements if possible. Keep it neat and honest. Do not exaggerate. If you have a bad year, explain why (drought, disease) and what you learned. Use a folder or a simple PDF on your phone. In Africa, many lenders like One Acre Fund, Equity Bank, and Kiva require specific formats. Ask them for a template. Also, SACCOs often accept handwritten records if they are consistent. Always keep a copy for yourself. A good report can get you lower interest rates or better terms. Practice presenting it in 5 minutes to a friend before submitting.

quiz.q: What is a Key Performance Indicator (KPI) on a farm?
options: B) A simple number that measures farm performance
quiz.explanation: KPIs are measurable values that show how well a farm is doing, such as yield per hectare.

quiz.q: If a farmer harvests 6 tonnes of maize from 2 hectares, what is the yield per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Yield per hectare = total harvest divided by hectares = 6/2 = 3 tonnes per hectare.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a variable cost in an enterprise budget?
quiz.explanation: Fertiliser is a variable cost because it changes with the level of production.

quiz.q: What does gross margin equal?
options: A) Total income minus total costs
B) Total income minus variable costs
C) Total income minus fixed costs
quiz.explanation: Gross margin is total income minus variable costs, showing profit before fixed costs.

quiz.q: In partial budgeting, which of the following is NOT one of the four columns?
quiz.explanation: Partial budgeting uses added income, reduced costs, added costs, and reduced income; fixed costs are not a column.

quiz.q: A farmer considers switching from local to hybrid maize seed. Extra cost is 10,000 KES, extra income is 60,000 KES. What is the net change?
quiz.explanation: Net change = added income (60,000) minus added costs (10,000) = +50,000 KES.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a cash flow projection?
options: B) To track when money comes in and goes out
C) To compare with industry averages
D) To apply for a loan
quiz.explanation: Cash flow projection shows the timing of cash inflows and outflows to avoid shortages.

quiz.q: Which of the following should be included in a cash flow projection?
quiz.explanation: Cash flow includes actual cash outflows like family living expenses, but not non-cash items like depreciation.

quiz.q: Benchmarking means:
options: B) Comparing your farm to industry averages
quiz.explanation: Benchmarking compares your performance to standards or averages in your area or industry.

quiz.q: If the average maize yield in your area is 2 tonnes per hectare and you get 1.5 tonnes, what does this indicate?
options: D) You need to switch crops
quiz.explanation: 1.5 tonnes is less than the 2-tonne average, so you are below average.

quiz.q: What should a report for a lender include?
options: B) Production records, financial statements, and repayment plan
D) A list of your neighbours
quiz.explanation: Lenders need production records, financial statements, and a repayment plan to assess risk.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use local benchmarks rather than international ones?
options: A) International benchmarks are always higher
B) Local conditions, costs, and yields differ
C) International benchmarks are not available
D) Local benchmarks are easier to find
quiz.explanation: Local benchmarks reflect the specific climate, soil, and market conditions of your area.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost in an enterprise budget?
quiz.explanation: Land rent is a fixed cost because it does not change with production level.

quiz.q: What is the first step in creating an enterprise budget?
quiz.explanation: You start by estimating expected income from the enterprise, then list costs.

quiz.q: In partial budgeting, if reduced costs are 10,000 KES and added costs are 8,000 KES, what is the net change from costs alone?
quiz.explanation: Net change from costs = reduced costs (10,000) minus added costs (8,000) = +2,000 KES.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of cash flow projection?
options: B) Shows when to arrange credit
quiz.explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash expense and is not part of cash flow projection.

quiz.q: A farmer has a negative net cash flow in February. What should they do?
options: B) Plan to delay purchases or arrange credit
quiz.explanation: A negative cash flow means more money going out than coming in; planning can help cover the gap.

quiz.q: What is a common source of benchmark data in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Local extension officers provide benchmarks relevant to African conditions.

quiz.q: If your cost per hectare is higher than the benchmark, what does it mean?
options: B) You are spending too much
C) You are spending too little
quiz.explanation: Higher cost per hectare than average indicates you may be overspending on inputs or labour.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a one-page summary in a report for lenders?
options: A) To replace all other records
B) To give a quick overview of your farm and request
C) To list all your expenses
D) To show your family photos
quiz.explanation: A one-page summary gives lenders a fast snapshot of your farm and what you need.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a KPI for a poultry farm?
options: A) Eggs per hen per year
C) Litres of milk per hectare
D) Tonnes of maize per cow
quiz.explanation: Eggs per hen per year is a common KPI for poultry production.

quiz.q: What is the formula for net profit in an enterprise budget?
options: A) Gross margin minus fixed costs
B) Gross margin plus fixed costs
C) Total income minus variable costs
D) Total income minus total costs
quiz.explanation: Net profit = gross margin (income minus variable costs) minus fixed costs.

quiz.q: In partial budgeting, if added income is 50,000 KES and reduced income is 20,000 KES, what is the net income change?
quiz.explanation: Net income change = added income (50,000) minus reduced income (20,000) = +30,000 KES.

quiz.q: Why is cash flow not the same as profit?
options: A) Because profit includes non-cash items
B) Because cash flow only tracks cash
quiz.explanation: Profit includes non-cash items like depreciation, while cash flow only tracks actual cash movements.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good practice when creating a cash flow projection?
options: C) Be conservative with income and costs
quiz.explanation: Being conservative (underestimate income, overestimate costs) helps avoid cash surprises.

quiz.q: What does a benchmark of 20 litres of milk per cow per day indicate?
options: B) A high standard for improved breeds
C) An average for local breeds
quiz.explanation: 20 litres per day is a high standard typical of improved dairy breeds with good management.

quiz.q: What should you do if your farm's performance is below benchmark?
options: C) Investigate why and set improvement targets
quiz.explanation: Identify the reasons for the gap and set realistic targets to improve.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical section in a report for investors?
quiz.explanation: Investors care about growth, returns, and financials, not personal preferences.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a copy of your report for yourself?
options: B) For your records and future reference
quiz.explanation: Keeping a copy helps you track what you submitted and learn for next time.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for recording KPIs?
quiz.explanation: A notebook is a simple, accessible tool for recording KPIs manually.

quiz.q: If a farmer's gross margin is 500,000 KES and fixed costs are 200,000 KES, what is net profit?
quiz.explanation: Net profit = gross margin (500,000) minus fixed costs (200,000) = 300,000 KES.
